{"status":"ok","message-type":"work-list","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"facets":{},"total-results":1602243,"items":[{"DOI":"10.1007/s10994-026-07031-z","title":["Empirical Gradient-Driven Continuous-Time SGD: Generalization Gap Dynamics and Practical Adaptive Training"],"author":[{"given":"Kai","family":"Cui","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]},{"given":"Wan","family":"Li","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,4]]},"container-title":["Machine Learning"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-026-07031-z","type":"journal-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>Momentum-based methods are commonly used in stochastic optimization to accelerate the training of deep learning models. Nevertheless, these methods may cause overshooting, primarily due to the accumulation of stochastic noise over iterations. The PID optimizer addresses this challenge by utilizing gradient difference information; however, it remains limited by the need for manual tuning of learning rates and momentum decay coefficients, constraining its applicability to deep neural networks (DNNs). This paper presents a comprehensive analytical framework for Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) based momentum gradient methods from a dynamical systems perspective, demonstrating linear convergence under regularity conditions for nonconvex objectives. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive double-parameter PID optimizer (AdaPID) that automatically adjusts both the learning rate and momentum decay using prior information, while formally establishing convergence rate guarantees for stochastic optimization. Numerical experiments using benchmark functions and real-world datasets demonstrate the improved robustness and performance of the proposed algorithm.</jats:p>","DOI":"10.36227/techrxiv.174612953.34891083/v1","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":1,"title":["AdaPID: Adaptive Momentum Gradient Method based on PID Controller for Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization in Deep Learning"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9971-6671","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Ailun","family":"Jian","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Xun","family":"Li","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Weigang","family":"Sun","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Gaohang","family":"Yu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2025,5,1]]},"URL":"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.174612953.34891083/v1"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>High-performance momentum gradient methods play a key role in speeding up the training of deep neural networks. Optimizers based on Discrete Proportional–Integral–Derivative (PID) controllers enhance training by reducing the risk of overshooting during momentum acceleration. However, their success largely depends on the manual tuning of the proportional coefficients in the P, I, and D components, which limits their practical application. Using control theory, we develop a unified analytical framework for PID-type momentum algorithms, establishing convergence conditions and parameter selection criteria under nonconvex objectives beyond Lipschitz smoothness. We further introduce an Adaptive Momentum Gradient Method based on PID Controller (AdaPID) and its stochastic variant AdaSPID, which adaptively adjust learning rates and momentum coefficients via modified Barzilai–Borwein steps and stochastic conjugate gradient directions, offering rigorous convergence guarantees in nonconvex stochastic settings.  Experiments on benchmark functions and image classification tasks demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed (INDIN)"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.1109/indin58382.2024.10774294","type":"proceedings-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>In order to increase prediction accuracy, deep learning models must be trained by adjusting parameters to
minimize a loss function. In supervised learning, the mapping between inputs and their right outputs is learned by training
models using labeled input examples. In order to minimize mistakes, predictions are compared to actual outcomes, and
optimization methods are used to adjust parameters. Until convergence is reached, these algorithms go through several
cycles of iteration. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Momentum SGD, RMSProp, AMSGrad, Adam, Yogi, and Lion are
the seven optimization techniques that are evaluated in this study based on training accuracy, test accuracy, training loss,
and sensitivity to learning rate. MNIST and CIFAR-10 were the two benchmark datasets used in the experiments. SGD with
a learning rate of 0.5 had the best test accuracy of 99.14% and the highest training accuracy of 99.89% on MNIST. With
test accuracy of 99.15% and 98%, respectively, at a learning rate of 1e-2, Momentum SGD and Adam likewise demonstrated
strong performance. Optimizers like Yogi and Lion, on the other hand, performed competitively at lower learning rates but
suffered at higher ones; at 1e-5, Lion's test accuracy was 98.69%. All optimizers displayed comparatively decreased
accuracies for CIFAR-10, which was indicative of the dataset's increased complexity. Momentum SGD outperformed other
optimizers including Adam, Yogi, and Lion, achieving the highest training accuracy of 98.90% and the best test accuracy of
72.94% at a learning rate of 1e-2. Lion showed better performance and stability on both datasets at a low learning rate of
1e-5. These results highlight how crucial it is to choose learning rates and optimization techniques that are specific to the
features of each dataset.</jats:p>","DOI":"10.38124/ijisrt/25aug007","type":"journal-article","is-referenced-by-count":3,"title":["Comparative Study of Deep Learning Optimizers: SGD, Momentum SGD,
